title: Dry-run: stateless services and service discovery

spec.title: Dry-run: stateless services and service discovery
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. Nothing here is hard code — the point is showing exactly what 'stateless' rules out and what replaces it.

steps.title: Stateful — breaks the moment you add a second instance
steps.explain: Storing session data in the process's own memory works with one instance and silently breaks with two: a user's second request can land on the instance that never saw their login.

steps.title: Fix: session state moves to a shared store
steps.explain: Moving session data to Redis means any instance can serve any request for that session — the app process itself holds nothing that would break if it were killed and replaced right now.
steps.saysOutLoud: Stateless means any instance can handle any request, which means state has to live somewhere shared.

steps.title: That statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling trivial
steps.explain: Because no instance holds anything unique, adding capacity is just adding more identical processes behind the load balancer — no data migration, no rebalancing, nothing to coordinate between the old and new instances.

steps.title: Instances register themselves on startup, not in config
steps.explain: Hardcoding a list of instance addresses breaks the moment autoscaling adds or removes one. Instead, each instance announces itself to a registry on boot and renews a lease periodically, so the registry always reflects who's actually alive right now.

steps.title: Clients discover instances by asking the registry, not DNS alone
steps.explain: Client-side discovery means the caller asks the registry for a live instance and load-balances locally, cutting out a hop through a separate LB tier — common inside a service mesh where every call is service-to-service.

steps.title: The registry itself is a piece of shared infrastructure
steps.explain: Consul, etcd, or a Kubernetes Service backed by kube-proxy all serve this role — a consistent, highly-available store of who's alive and where, that every service instance reads from and writes its own heartbeat to.

spec.closing: If they ask what CAN live in an instance's own memory: a request-scoped cache is fine — anything that only needs to exist for the duration of one request never crosses instance boundaries and never needs to be shared.
